title: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
summary: Why models that read raw UTF-8 bytes avoid tokenizer blind spots, why that is costly, and how MegaByte, SpaceByte, BLT and H-Net group bytes into patches or learned chunks to make it scale.
outcomes: Explain why byte-level models cost more per byte and why feed-forward layers, not attention, dominate that cost
Compute forward FLOPs per byte for a patched model from global and local parameter counts
Convert a GPT to bytes and to a MegaByte-style patch model, and compute bits per byte from a token-level loss
Apply entropy patching with global and monotonic thresholds, and calibrate a threshold to a target patch size
Describe BLT's encoder, latent Transformer and decoder, including the one-patch shift that keeps decoding causal
Trace BLT generation byte by byte and explain why equal FLOPs need not mean equal latency
Weigh byte models against BPE on compute, robustness and character-level tasks
Compare BLT's separate entropy model with learned chunking (H-Net) and earlier character-level designs

lessons.title: Why drop the tokenizer, and why raw bytes are expensive

blocks.md: A GPT, as you built it, never sees text. A **tokenizer** first maps the text to ids from a fixed vocabulary learned by BPE, and the model only ever sees those ids. The Byte Latent Transformer (BLT) paper (Pagnoni et al., 2024, from Meta), the main paper of this course, lists what this costs: models are sensitive to domain shifts (text unlike the data they were trained on) and to noisy input, they lack *orthographic* knowledge (how words are spelled), and they are inequitable across languages because the vocabulary was fitted mostly to some languages.

The token id for `strawberry` carries no explicit trace of its letters. To count the r's, the model must have memorized the spelling of that id. A **tokenizer-free** model removes the fixed vocabulary and reads the raw **bytes** of the text instead, so every letter is in its input.

Text on disk is almost always **UTF-8**, which encodes each Unicode character (code point) as 1 to 4 bytes (defined in RFC 3629, one of the Request for Comments documents that hold internet standards). ASCII characters take 1 byte. Every other character starts with a *lead byte* followed by *continuation bytes* of the form `10xxxxxx`. The leading 1 bits of the lead byte count the bytes of the character (`110` for 2, `1110` for 3, `11110` for 4), and the x positions carry the bits of the code point. A byte model therefore needs only 256 input ids, can represent any string in any language, and never sees an unknown token.

blocks.title: The same words as UTF-8 bytes (hex)

scenes.caption: English letters are ASCII, 1 byte each: hello is 5 characters and 5 bytes. A byte model with 256 input ids reads this directly.
In café, the accented e is one character but 2 bytes (c3 a9): a lead byte plus one continuation byte. 4 characters become 5 bytes.
Cyrillic takes 2 bytes per character and Japanese 3, so 6 Russian characters are 12 bytes and 3 Japanese characters are 9. Colors alternate per character.
Devanagari code points take 3 bytes each: this Hindi word is 6 code points and 18 bytes. Byte sequences are longest exactly where subword vocabularies are usually weakest.

blocks.prompt: A Transformer spends roughly the same compute on every position it processes. Llama 3's tokenizer averages about 4.4 bytes per token on BLT's training mix. If you feed the same text as raw bytes to a model with the same parameters, roughly how much more compute does it spend?
blocks.reveal: About **4.4 times** more, because there are about 4.4 times more positions. The extra cost is not mainly attention: a forward pass with $m$ non-embedding parameters over $T$ positions costs roughly $2mT$ FLOPs (the approximation MegaByte uses), and that term is linear in $T$. Making each position cheaper or making fewer positions is the only way out.

blocks.md: Where does $2mT$ come from? Almost every parameter is a weight in a matrix that multiplies each position's vector once, which costs one multiply and one add per weight: 2 FLOPs per parameter per position, so $2m$ per position and $2mT$ for $T$ positions. **Non-embedding parameters** are all weights except the embedding tables; looking up an embedding row is a memory read, not a multiply, so it costs almost no FLOPs. Attention scores add a term that grows with $T^2$, but at this scale it is small.

blocks.caption: m = non-embedding parameters, T = number of positions. Per-position feed-forward and projection layers dominate: MegaByte notes self-attention is only 1.4% of GPT-3's FLOPs.

blocks.md: Common misconception: byte models are slow because attention is quadratic. Efficient attention (methods and kernels such as FlashAttention that make attention cheaper or faster) helps small models, but the BLT authors point out that at scale the cost is dominated by the large feed-forward layers that run on **every** position. Fewer positions through the big network is what matters.

**ByT5** (Xue et al., 2022) showed the simplest approach works. It starts from T5 (Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer, Raffel et al., 2020), an **encoder-decoder** Transformer: an encoder reads the whole input with no causal mask, and a decoder generates the output one id at a time while also attending to the encoder's outputs. ByT5 feeds it UTF-8 bytes with 256 byte ids plus 3 special ids (padding, which fills short sequences up to a common length, end of sequence, and an unused UNK), and keeps everything else standard.

Two changes helped: the parameters freed from the vocabulary matrices went into the layers, and the encoder was made 3 times deeper than the decoder. The vocabulary matrices are the input embedding table and the output matrix that scores every vocabulary entry before the softmax; each has one row per entry, so a large vocabulary makes them huge. T5 pre-trains by span corruption: random spans (short stretches) of the input are replaced by placeholder ids, and the model learns to output the missing text. Its pre-training masks spans of about 20 bytes instead of about 3 tokens. So a masked span still covers a few words, not a few letters. The baseline is mT5, the multilingual T5, with a 250,000-entry subword vocabulary.

blocks.title: Share of parameters in the vocabulary matrices

scenes.caption: mT5 (multilingual subword vocabulary): the vocabulary and softmax matrices take 85% of the Small model and 66% of the 582M-parameter Base model.
ByT5 at the same total size: the 256-byte vocabulary is at most 0.3% of parameters at every size, so almost all capacity sits in the Transformer layers.

blocks.md: The price was speed. ByT5 reports inference 3.7 to 6.4 times slower than mT5 on document summarization and 6.4 to 9.5 times slower on XNLI classification, where inputs are long and outputs are short. XNLI (Cross-lingual Natural Language Inference) gives a pair of sentences in one of 15 languages and asks whether the first implies, contradicts or is neutral toward the second. Every byte goes through every layer. The rest of this course is about avoiding that.

Bytes remove the vocabulary and its blind spots, but multiply the number of positions by roughly 4. Since compute is about $2mT$, a byte model is only practical if the big network runs on far fewer positions than there are bytes.

blocks.question: A team swaps a 128K BPE vocabulary for raw bytes and keeps the same 7B Transformer, using FlashAttention for speed. Training throughput in bytes per second drops about 4x. What is the main reason?
options: FlashAttention does not support a vocabulary of 256
Attention is quadratic, so 4x longer sequences cost 16x more
There are about 4x more positions and the feed-forward and projection layers run once per position
The 256-way softmax is more expensive than a 128K-way softmax
blocks.explain: Compute scales roughly as 2mT, linear in the number of positions T. With about 4 bytes per token there are about 4x more positions, so throughput per byte drops about 4x. Attention is a small share at this scale, and a 256-way softmax is far cheaper than a 128K-way one.

blocks.question: Why can a byte-level model never hit an out-of-vocabulary input?
options: Its vocabulary is the 256 possible byte values, and any UTF-8 text is a sequence of bytes
It learns new tokens during inference
It maps rare characters to an UNK id
UTF-8 has only 256 characters
blocks.explain: Every string, in any script, is a sequence of bytes 0 to 255, so the input vocabulary is complete by construction. UTF-8 covers all of Unicode by using 1 to 4 bytes per character, not by having 256 characters.

lessons.title: Patches: run the big model once per group of bytes

blocks.md: **MegaByte** (Yu et al., 2023) groups bytes into **patches** of a fixed size $P$. A large **global** Transformer runs once per patch, over $T/P$ positions, and a small **local** Transformer predicts the $P$ bytes inside each patch, one byte at a time, conditioned on the global output. Most bytes are easy (finishing a word after its first letters), so the expensive network is not needed for every byte.

blocks.caption: From MegaByte's analysis: m_g = global parameters, m_l = local parameters, T = bytes. When m_g is much larger than m_l, the cost falls almost as 1/P.

blocks.md: The formula follows from lesson 1's $2m$ FLOPs per position. The global model's $m_g$ parameters run on only $T/P$ positions, costing $2m_gT/P$, and the local model's $m_\ell$ parameters run on all $T$ bytes, costing $2m_\ell T$. Adding the two and taking out the common factor $2T$ gives the formula.

Attention gets cheaper too. The global model attends over $T/P$ positions, costing $O(T^2/P^2)$, and the local model runs $T/P$ sequences of length $P$, costing $O(TP)$. Choosing $P = T^{1/3}$ gives $O(T^{4/3})$ overall. That choice balances the two terms: $T^2/P^2 = TP$ exactly when $P^3 = T$, and then each term is $T^{4/3}$. But as lesson 1 showed, the feed-forward savings matter more. In BLT the global and local parts are joined by **cross-attention**: attention whose queries come from one sequence and whose keys and values come from another, here bytes and patches (lesson 5 shows it in detail).

MegaByte joins its two models more simply, and the join is what keeps it causal. The global input for patch $k$ is the concatenation of the $P$ byte embeddings of patch $k-1$ (a learned padding patch stands in for $k = 0$), so the global output for patch $k$ has seen only earlier patches. That output is split into $P$ slices, each projected to the local width and **added** to the local model's input at one byte position of patch $k$. The local inputs are the patch's own bytes shifted right by one (a learned padding byte first), so the local model predicts byte $p$ from bytes before it. Lesson 3 builds this and shows what breaks without the shift.

blocks.title: Forward FLOPs per byte versus patch size

scenes.caption: Simplified model (ignores attention and cross-attention). Defaults match BLT's 8B config: 6.4B global, 20M encoder plus 120M decoder local parameters. Without patching every byte costs 13.08 GFLOPs (billion FLOPs).
At P = 4.4 (Llama 3's bytes per token) the cost is 3.19 GFLOPs per byte; at P = 8 it is 1.88, 41% less. The local term 2 m_l = 0.28 is a floor that patching cannot remove.

Grow the global model to 8B: now P = 4.4 costs 3.92 and P = 8 costs 2.28 (the marked points stay at 6.4B). 8B at P = 8 is still cheaper than 6.4B at P = 4.4: longer patches buy room for a bigger model.

blocks.md: Fixed-size patches have two problems, according to the BLT paper. Compute is not spent where it is needed: a whole global step may go to predicting whitespace in code, while dense text such as math gets too little. And patching is not contextual: the same word is split differently depending on where it lands.

blocks.title: Three ways to cut the same 22 bytes

scenes.caption: Strided patching (MegaByte) every 4 bytes gives 6 patches. The first the is one patch, but the second is cut into on_t and he_m: the same word looks different to the global model each time.
Space patching (SpaceByte) starts a patch after each space-like byte, so every word gets its own global step: 6 patches, and both copies of the are cut identically.
Preview: entropy patching with a toy model (lesson 4) gives 5 patches. It merges on_the_ into one patch because the whole phrase is predictable after on.

blocks.md: **SpaceByte** (Slagle, 2024) calls a byte *space-like* if it is not a Latin letter, a digit, or a UTF-8 continuation byte, and inserts larger Transformer blocks in the middle of a byte-level Transformer, applied only after space-like bytes, while the small blocks run on every byte. The hardest byte to predict is usually the first of a word, so this spends compute where it is needed. But it cannot vary the patch size, and it does not fit languages and domains without clear spaces.

Why not just use longer BPE tokens? A bigger vocabulary makes tokens longer, but it also grows the embedding table and the output softmax. The BLT paper notes Llama 3 raised the average token from 3.7 to 4.4 bytes at the cost of a 4x larger embedding table (its vocabulary grew from 32,000 to about 128,000 entries). A **patch** has no vocabulary at all: a small encoder network (lesson 5) turns any byte group into a vector, so patch size is a free knob.
A patch is a group of bytes that the big model treats as one position, with no fixed vocabulary. Average patch size sets the compute: forward cost per byte is about $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$.

blocks.question: Using the simplified cost $2(m_g/P + m_\ell)$ with $m_g$ = 6.4B and $m_\ell$ = 0.14B, what is the forward cost per byte at $P$ = 6?
options: About 13.1 GFLOPs
About 1.07 GFLOPs
About 2.41 GFLOPs
About 3.19 GFLOPs
blocks.explain: 2 x (6.4/6 + 0.14) = 2 x (1.067 + 0.14) = 2.41 GFLOPs. 13.1 is the unpatched cost, 3.19 is P = 4.4, and 1.07 forgets the factor 2 and the local term.

blocks.question: Which weakness is shared by strided and space patching but fixed by a patcher driven by prediction difficulty?
options: Both need a fixed vocabulary
Neither can split a word into more than one patch
Neither lets you tune the average patch size
Neither decides boundaries from how hard the upcoming bytes are to predict
blocks.explain: Strided patching cuts every P bytes, and space patching cuts at spaces; neither looks at how predictable the text is. Strided patching does let you tune P (so the third option is wrong for it), and neither uses a vocabulary.

lessons.title: Build it: a byte GPT, then a two-level patch model

blocks.md: Time to change real code. Start from the GPT you built in the *Build a GPT from scratch* course. A BPE GPT turns `hi` into one or two token ids from a learned vocabulary; a byte GPT turns it into `[104, 105]`, the two UTF-8 bytes, and nothing else. Three things change: the encoder becomes `text.encode("utf-8")`, the vocabulary size becomes 256 (so the embedding table and output head shrink), and decoding must cope with byte sequences that are not valid UTF-8. The Transformer blocks stay exactly as they were. How BPE builds its vocabulary is taught in the *Tokenization with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE)* course; here we only replace it.

blocks.code:
text = "café au lait"
ids = list(text.encode("utf-8"))        # the whole tokenizer
print(len(text), len(ids), ids[:5])     # 12 13 [99, 97, 102, 195, 169]
print(bytes(ids).decode("utf-8"))       # café au lait
sampled = ids[:4] + [32]                # model put a space after the lead byte c3
print(bytes(sampled).decode("utf-8", errors="replace"))   # 'caf\ufffd '
try:
    bytes(sampled).decode("utf-8")      # strict decoding raises
except UnicodeDecodeError as e:
    print(e.reason)                     # invalid continuation byte

cfg = GPTConfig(vocab_size=256, block_size=512)   # nothing else changes
blocks.caption: Run with Python 3; outputs shown as comments. The printed replacement character U+FFFD is written here as its escape.

blocks.md: Why can a sample be invalid? The model picks one byte at a time from a 256-way softmax, and nothing in the sampler knows UTF-8. After the lead byte `c3` (binary `110` prefix, so one continuation byte must follow) it can still pick a space, or it can emit a continuation byte `10xxxxxx` with no lead byte before it. Decoding with `errors="replace"` turns each broken sequence into U+FFFD, the Unicode replacement character, while the default strict mode raises an error. A well-trained model rarely does this, but a streaming UI must hold back an incomplete character until its last byte arrives. Byte-level BPE has the same issue at token boundaries (BPE course, lesson 5).

To compare a byte model with a BPE model you need one score with the same unit. **Bits per byte** (BPB) is the total cross-entropy over a text, converted from nats to bits by dividing by $\ln 2$, divided by the number of bytes in that text. For a token model, sum the loss of every token, then divide by the bytes those tokens cover, not by the token count. Worked number: a token loss of 3.0 nats at 4.4 bytes per token is $3.0 / (\ln 2 \times 4.4) = 0.98$ bits per byte.

blocks.caption: l_t = loss in nats of position t. For a byte model n_bytes equals the number of positions, so BPB is simply the mean loss divided by ln 2.

blocks.code:
tot = 0.0                                   # summed loss in nats
for x, y in val_windows():                  # non-overlapping windows
    tot += F.cross_entropy(model(x).flatten(0, 1), y.flatten(),
                           reduction='sum').item()
if bpe:   # bytes covered by every scored target token
    n_bytes = tok_bytes[scored_targets].sum()
else:     # one position per byte
    n_bytes = n_scored_positions
bpb = tot / (math.log(2) * n_bytes)
blocks.caption: The conversion used for every number in this lesson. tok_bytes[i] is the byte length of token id i.

blocks.md: Now the two-level model, MegaByte style, with a fixed patch size $P = 4$. Embed each byte at width $D_G = 64$, reshape the sequence into patches, and concatenate the 4 byte embeddings of a patch into one 256-wide vector. Prepend a learned padding patch and drop the last patch: this **one-patch shift** means global position $k$ holds patch $k-1$. Run a causal global Transformer (width 256) over the patches. Split each global output into 4 slices of 64, project each to the local width 128, and add slice $p$ to the local input at byte $p$ of patch $k$. The local input is the byte embedding of the *previous* byte in the patch (a learned padding vector at $p = 0$). A small causal local Transformer runs inside each patch and predicts all 4 bytes.

blocks.title: The two shifts in a MegaByte-style model (P = 4)

scenes.caption: The bytes the model must predict, in 3 patches of 4. Every byte, including the first, is a target, because the shifts below are built into the inputs.
Global input is shifted by one whole patch: the global step for patch 1 (targets c a t _) receives the bytes of patch 0. It can summarize the past but cannot see any of its own targets.

Local input is shifted by one byte inside each patch: to predict a it gets c, to predict t it gets a. The first byte of a patch gets a padding vector plus the global output, nothing from its own patch.
Drop the global shift and patch 1's global step receives c a t _ itself: the local model can copy its targets. That is the leak measured below.

blocks.code:
def forward(self, x, tgt):                   # x: (B, T) bytes, T = K * P
    B, T = x.shape; P = self.P; K = T // P
    h = self.g_emb(x) + self.g_pos(torch.arange(T, device=x.device))
    patches = h.view(B, K, -1)                # concat P byte embeddings
    patches = torch.cat([self.g_pad.expand(B, 1, -1),
                         patches[:, :-1]], 1) # shift by one patch
    g = self.g_ln(self.glob(patches))         # (B, K, P*D_G)
    g = self.w_gl(g.view(B, K, P, -1))        # slice p to local width
    e = self.l_emb(x).view(B, K, P, -1)
    e = torch.cat([self.l_pad.expand(B, K, 1, -1),
                   e[:, :, :-1]], 2)          # shift by one byte
    y = self.loc((g + e).view(B * K, P, -1))  # K independent patches
    logits = self.head(self.ln(y))            # 256-way, every byte
    return F.cross_entropy(logits.flatten(0, 1), tgt.flatten())
blocks.caption: The forward pass of the model trained below (the script sums the loss for bits per byte; shown here as a mean). Targets are the input bytes themselves: the shifts already make it next-byte prediction.

blocks.md: **The experiment.** Data: the first 60 MB of enwik8 (a 100 MB dump of English Wikipedia XML, a standard byte-level benchmark) for training and 1 MB from its validation region. The BPE model uses a 4096-entry byte-level BPE vocabulary trained with the Hugging Face tokenizers library on the first 10 MB, giving 2.88 bytes per token on the training text. All three models share the same core: 4 blocks of width 256 with 4 heads, about 3.2M non-embedding parameters. Each sees about 512 bytes of context: 178 BPE tokens, 512 bytes, or 128 patches of 4. MegaByte adds a 2-block, width-128 local model. Each gets the same training budget of 6 x 10^14 FLOPs, counted per position as $2N + 2 n_{layer} n_{ctx} d$ forward (Kaplan et al.; here $N$ also counts the output head, $d$ x vocabulary), times 3 to include the backward pass.

blocks.title: Equal training FLOPs on enwik8 (small models, one run each)

scenes.caption: Validation bits per byte after 6 x 10^14 training FLOPs: 1.797 for BPE, 2.592 for the byte GPT, 2.073 for MegaByte. Lower is better.
Training steps the budget buys at 32 sequences per step: 4011, 1633 and 4865. The byte GPT pays for 512 positions per sequence in the big network, about 2.5 times the BPE cost per step.

Training bytes seen, in millions: 65.7, 26.8 and 79.7. At equal FLOPs the byte GPT reads far less text; MegaByte's global model runs once per 4 bytes, so it reads even more than BPE (79.7 against 65.7).
Measured milliseconds per training step on an Apple M-series GPU (MPS), shared with other jobs, so treat these as rough: 57.6, 163.1, 72.0.

blocks.md: What the toy shows: at equal FLOPs, the byte GPT is far behind (2.59 against 1.80 bits per byte), because every byte runs through the whole network and the budget buys only 27 MB of text. Patching recovers most of that gap: MegaByte reaches 2.07 with the same core network and reads more text than the BPE model. What it cannot show: these are 3M-parameter models, one run each, trained on 27 to 80 MB, so the ranking says nothing about whether patches beat tokens at scale. The BLT and MegaByte claims come from models 100 to 2,000 times larger trained on far more data, and their crossovers appear only there. The point of the lab is the mechanics: the vocabulary swap, the bits-per-byte conversion and the shifts.

The shift is the step reimplementations most often get wrong, and the bug looks like success. The same MegaByte model with the global shift removed reached essentially 0 validation bits per byte (below 0.0001) after 810 steps: a perfect score, because the global step for each patch was fed that patch's own bytes and the local model learned to copy them. A loss that is suddenly too good is a leak until proven otherwise.

A byte GPT is a GPT with a 256-entry vocabulary; the cost is more positions per byte. A two-level model fixes that by running the big network once per patch, and stays causal only through two shifts: one patch for the global input, one byte for the local input.

blocks.question: A BPE model has a validation loss of 2.5 nats per token at 4.0 bytes per token. A byte model reaches 0.95 bits per byte on the same text. Which predicts the text better?
options: The BPE model, because 2.5 nats per token converts to about 0.90 bits per byte
The byte model, because 0.95 is smaller than 2.5
They cannot be compared, because one is per token and one is per byte
The byte model, because bits are smaller units than nats
blocks.explain: 2.5 / (ln 2 x 4.0) = 2.5 / 2.77 = 0.90 bits per byte, which is below 0.95. Converting both to bits per byte is exactly what makes them comparable; comparing 2.5 with 0.95 directly mixes units.

blocks.question: In the MegaByte model above, the local model predicts byte 2 of patch 5. Which information may it use?
options: Bytes 0 to 3 of patch 5 and the global output for patch 5
Only bytes 0 and 1 of patch 5
All bytes of patches 0 to 5
Bytes 0 and 1 of patch 5, plus the global output computed from patches 0 to 4
blocks.explain: The global input at position 5 holds patch 4, so the causal global output there summarizes patches 0 to 4. Inside the patch, the one-byte shift and the causal local mask give bytes 0 and 1. Byte 3 and byte 2 itself are hidden.

lessons.title: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard

blocks.md: BLT's answer is **entropy patching**: train a small byte-level language model $p_e$, and start a new patch wherever it is uncertain about the next byte. Uncertainty is measured by the **entropy** of its next-byte distribution. A peaked distribution (the next byte is obvious) has low entropy; a flat one has high entropy. Write $H(x_i)$ for this entropy at byte position $i$: how unsure $p_e$ is about byte $i$, given only the bytes before it.

blocks.tex: H(x_i) = -\sum_{v \in \mathcal{V}} p_e(x_i = v \mid x_{<i}) \, \ln p_e(x_i = v \mid x_{<i})
blocks.caption: Next-byte entropy over the byte vocabulary V. The released BLT code computes it in nats (natural log). The maximum, for a uniform distribution over 256 bytes, is ln 256 = 5.55 nats.

blocks.md: In words: for every possible next byte $v$, take its probability $p$, multiply it by $-\ln p$ (the surprise if $v$ occurs), and add these up. So entropy is the average surprise, the cross-entropy loss you know but averaged under the model's own prediction instead of the true byte. If one byte has probability 1, its surprise is $\ln 1 = 0$ and the entropy is zero. If all 256 bytes have probability 1/256, each term is $\frac{1}{256}\ln 256$, and the 256 terms add up to $\ln 256 = 5.55$ nats, the maximum.

To see it on real numbers, we use a toy entropy model: counts of the next byte given the previous 2 bytes, trained on a 147-byte corpus about cats, dogs and mats, with add-0.05 smoothing over the 15 distinct bytes in that corpus. Smoothing adds 0.05 to the count of each of the 15 bytes before dividing by the total, so a byte never seen after a context still gets a small probability instead of zero. BLT's actual entropy model is a 100M-parameter Transformer (14 layers, hidden size 512, 512-byte sliding window). A sliding window means each position attends only to the previous 512 bytes, so the cost per byte stays fixed however long the text is.

blocks.code:
from collections import Counter, defaultdict
import math
corpus = (b"the cat sat on the mat. the dog sat on the log. "
          b"a cat and a dog sat on a mat. the cat ate the rat. "
          b"the rat sat on the hat. on the mat the cat sat. ")
alphabet = sorted(set(corpus))          # 15 distinct bytes
counts = defaultdict(Counter)
for i in range(len(corpus)):
    counts[corpus[max(0, i - 2):i]][corpus[i]] += 1

def entropy(ctx, k=0.05):
    c = counts[ctx]; n = sum(c.values())
    ps = [(c[v] + k) / (n + k * len(alphabet)) for v in alphabet]
    return -sum(p * math.log(p) for p in ps)

print(round(entropy(b"e "), 2), round(entropy(b"ca"), 2))  # 2.01 0.81
blocks.caption: Toy 2-byte-context entropy model used for every number in this lesson.

blocks.title: Toy model: next-byte probabilities

scenes.caption: After the e and space of the, many words can follow. The mass is spread over c, m, r and more: entropy 2.01 nats. This is a hard prediction, worth a global step.
After ca, the corpus only ever continued with t, so t gets 0.853 and the rest is smoothing: entropy 0.81 nats. The local model can handle this byte cheaply.

blocks.md: Given entropies, BLT tests two boundary rules. The **global constraint** starts a patch at byte $t$ when $H(x_t)$ exceeds a threshold $\theta_g$. The **approximate monotonic constraint** starts one when entropy *jumps* by more than $\theta_r$ from the previous byte, so a patch is a stretch where entropy is roughly decreasing.

blocks.caption: Global rule: byte t starts a patch when its entropy is above theta_g. Monotonic rule: byte t starts a patch when its entropy is higher than the previous byte's by more than theta_r.

blocks.title: Entropy patching on the cat sat on the mat

scenes.caption: Toy-model entropy of each byte given the 2 bytes before it (the text follows a previous sentence ending in a period and space). Peaks sit at word starts: c and m at 2.01, s and o at 1.54.

Global threshold 1.6: only bytes above it start patches (red; the first byte, at 1.45, is red because it always starts one). 3 patches: the_, then cat_sat_on_the_ as one long patch, then mat. Average 7.3 bytes per patch.
Threshold 1.2: s and o now also qualify. 5 patches (the_, cat_, sat_, on_the_, mat), average 4.4 bytes. Note on_the_ stays together: after on_ the toy model is fairly sure what comes.
Threshold 0.9: spaces (1.05), a and t of mat (0.97) and t of the (1.09) also cross it. 10 patches, average 2.2 bytes: more global steps, more compute.
Monotonic rule with a jump threshold of 0.3 instead: a patch starts when entropy rises by more than 0.3 over the previous byte. 7 patches: the_, cat_, sat, the lone space _, on_, the_, mat.

blocks.prompt: In the threshold 1.2 scene, the second the is not its own patch, but the first the is. Why does the global model get no separate step for the second the?
blocks.reveal: Patch starts depend on context, not on the word. The first the begins the text, and position 0 always starts a patch. The second follows on_, and the toy model sees only the last 2 bytes, n_, which the corpus continues with t 4 times out of 5, so this t has entropy 1.09, below 1.2. The model judges it predictable and lets the local layers handle it inside the on_the_ patch.

blocks.md: The threshold is a dial on compute. BLT picks it to hit a target average patch size on the training mix, and keeps bytes per batch constant across settings so larger patches do not get an unfair advantage in context. For its 8B entropy-patched model the authors also changed the threshold at inference from 0.6 to 0.1, which improved task scores at the cost of more global steps.

blocks.title: Average patch size as the global threshold rises

scenes.caption: The 22 bytes of the cat sat on the mat, toy-model entropies from above. Each bar is bytes per patch at that threshold. Low thresholds cut almost every byte: 1.38 bytes per patch at 0.5.

The curve is a staircase because this tiny model produces only a few distinct entropy values. Any threshold from 1.09 up to just below 1.54 gives exactly 5 patches, 4.4 bytes each, the target in this course.

At 2.1 no byte qualifies, so the whole text is one patch (only position 0 starts one). On a real training mix with millions of bytes the staircase becomes a smooth curve and the target can be hit closely.

blocks.code:
def avg_patch(H, th):              # global rule; byte 0 always starts
    starts = 1 + sum(h > th for h in H[1:])
    return len(H) / starts

def calibrate(H, target, lo=0.0, hi=5.55):
    for _ in range(40):            # bisection: size grows with th
        mid = (lo + hi) / 2
        lo, hi = (mid, hi) if avg_patch(H, mid) < target else (lo, mid)
    return hi

for th in (0.5, 0.9, 1.2, 1.6):
    print(th, round(avg_patch(H, th), 2))   # 1.38  2.2  4.4  7.33
print(round(calibrate(H, 4.4), 2))         # 1.09
blocks.caption: H is the list of 22 entropies above. Calibrating means finding the smallest threshold whose average patch size reaches the target, measured on a sample of the training mix (here, one sentence).

blocks.md: Where does $p_e$ itself come from? It is an ordinary byte-level language model, trained first with the usual next-byte cross-entropy on the same data distribution as BLT. It is then used as a fixed tool: patch boundaries are computed while loading data, and BLT's own gradients never reach it. The paper lists this separate training as a limitation and names end-to-end learned patching as future work; lesson 8 covers models that do exactly that. Its ablation found that entropy models beyond about 50M parameters with a 512-byte context gave diminishing returns.

Patching must also work during generation, when future bytes do not exist yet. BLT calls a scheme **incremental** if patching a prefix gives the same boundaries as patching the full text and then truncating. Entropy patching is incremental because $H(x_t)$ depends only on earlier bytes. BPE is not: the same prefix can be tokenized differently depending on what follows.

blocks.caption: Incremental patching property from the BLT paper: patching only the bytes before position i gives the same boundaries as patching the whole text x and then keeping the part before i. f_p is the patching function.

blocks.md: Entropy depends on context, which can backfire. On a few-shot prompt (several solved examples before the question) for MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, multiple choice on 57 subjects), repeated phrases became very predictable, so they were swallowed into huge patches (the paper calls this entropy drift). The fix for the large run: reset the entropy model's context at newlines and use the monotonic rule.
Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

blocks.question: You lower the global entropy threshold from 1.2 to 0.9 in the toy example. What happens?
options: Patch count drops from 5 to 3, saving compute
Patches get shorter (10 instead of 5), so the global model runs twice as often
Nothing changes, because boundaries come from spaces
The local decoder's vocabulary grows
blocks.explain: More bytes exceed a lower threshold, so more patches start: 10 patches of 2.2 bytes on average instead of 5 of 4.4. Each patch is one global step, so global compute roughly doubles. Raising the threshold (to 1.6) is what gives 3 patches.

blocks.question: Why can BPE tokenization not be used to decide patch boundaries while generating byte by byte?
options: BPE needs a GPU
BPE vocabularies are too small
BPE boundaries for a prefix can change once later bytes arrive, so it is not incremental
BPE only works on ASCII
blocks.explain: During generation BLT must decide whether the current byte starts a patch before future bytes exist. Entropy uses only past bytes, so its decisions never change. BPE merges depend on what follows, so the same prefix can be split differently.

lessons.title: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder

blocks.md: BLT has three Transformer parts. A small **local encoder** turns bytes into patch vectors. A large **latent (global) Transformer** runs once per patch. It is called latent because it never sees bytes, only patch vectors, which are learned internal representations. A small **local decoder** turns patch outputs back into next-byte predictions. A separate entropy model only decides where patches start.

blocks.title: BLT data flow

scenes.caption: Step 1: the entropy model reads the bytes and marks patch starts. This runs during data loading in training, separate from the main model.
Step 2: each byte gets an embedding plus hashed n-gram embeddings, then a light encoder layer. Cross-attention pools the bytes of each patch into one patch vector.
Step 3: the latent Transformer, nearly all of the parameters, runs once per patch with a causal mask over patches. This is where the compute savings come from.
Step 4: the local decoder lets byte states query the latent output of the previous patch through cross-attention, then predicts each next byte with a 256-way softmax.

blocks.md: **Hash n-gram embeddings.** One byte carries little meaning, so the encoder also looks at the byte n-grams ending at each position, for $n$ from 3 to 8. Storing an embedding for every possible n-gram is impossible, so each n-gram is hashed into a fixed-size table $E_n^{hash}$, one table per $n$, and the looked-up vectors are added to the byte embedding $x_i$. Different n-grams can collide in a slot; the tables are large enough that this is tolerable.

blocks.caption: g_{i,n} = the n bytes ending at position i; a = a 10-digit prime. The sum is normalized by the number of n-gram sizes plus one before entering the encoder.

blocks.md: In words: position $i$'s input vector $e_i$ is its byte embedding $x_i$ plus one looked-up row from each table $E_3$ to $E_8$. The row number is a polynomial hash of the n-gram: multiply the newest byte by $a^0$, the byte before it by $a^1$, and so on, add the products, and keep the remainder after dividing by the table size.

blocks.title: Hashing the n-grams that end at the t of cat
blocks.code:
a = 1000000007          # a 10-digit prime
E = 500000              # slots per n-gram table
s = b"the cat sat"
i = 6                   # byte t of cat (0-based)
for n in range(3, 9):
    if i + 1 < n:       # not enough history
        continue
    gram = s[i - n + 1 : i + 1]
    h = sum(s[i - j + 1] * a ** (j - 1)
            for j in range(1, n + 1))
    slot = h % E        # row of table E_n

scenes.caption: Position 6 of the cat sat is the t of cat. n = 3 gives the 3-gram cat; its polynomial hash mod 500,000 lands in slot 5646 of table E_3.
n = 4 includes the space before cat, drawn as an underscore: _cat hashes to slot 16622 of E_4, a separate table.
n = 5, 6, 7 add more history: e_cat to 259123, he_cat to 7051, the_cat to 154335. Each lookup adds a vector to the byte embedding.

n = 8 needs 8 bytes but only 7 exist up to position 6, so it is skipped (the paper omits n-grams longer than the history). The released code instead zero-pads, offsets byte ids by 4 and gives the oldest byte weight a^0, so its slots differ.

blocks.md: The paper uses 500,000 hash slots per table with n-gram sizes 3 to 8. Its experiments report **bits per byte** (lesson 3; lower is better). In a 1B-parameter ablation, an experiment that removes or changes one component to measure its effect, the hash embeddings gave large gains in bits per byte, the per-n-gram table size mattered most, and smaller n-grams helped more than larger ones. At 8B, going from 500K to 300K slots changed bits per byte by only 0.001.

**Pooling bytes into patches.** The encoder uses cross-attention in the style of the Perceiver: each patch is a query, initialized by max-pooling the byte states in that patch, and the keys and values are byte states. The Perceiver (Jaegle et al., 2021) has a small set of query vectors cross-attend to a much larger input, so the cost grows with the small set; here the small set is the patches. Max-pooling takes, for each dimension, the largest value among the byte states of the patch. A mask lets each patch attend **only to its own bytes**. Patch vectors are wider than byte vectors, so each patch gets $k$ query vectors of byte width, whose outputs are concatenated and projected to the global width (the shapes follow).

blocks.title: Encoder cross-attention mask: which bytes each patch can see

scenes.caption: Using the threshold 1.2 patches of the cat sat: 3 patches over 11 bytes (the 1-byte start patch the code adds, shown in the decoder figure below, is left out). A 1 means the patch query may attend to that byte. The mask is block-diagonal.
The cat_ patch attends only to bytes 4 to 7. Its query starts as the max-pool of those 4 byte states, and attention then refines it.
The last patch has 3 bytes. Patches vary in length, which is why the authors used PyTorch FlexAttention, which compiles a mask written as a small function into a fast attention kernel.

blocks.md:
**Following one patch through the 8B model** (paper Table 10 and the released code; $k = 4$ for this size):

1. The patch's $n$ bytes leave the 1-layer encoder as $n$ vectors of width $h_E = 1280$.
2. Max-pooling gives one 1280-vector; a linear map widens it to $k \times 1280 = 5120$, read as 4 query vectors of 1280.
3. Cross-attention with 20 heads of 64 dimensions ($20 \times 64 = 1280$): each of the 4 queries attends to the $n$ byte states of its own patch.
4. The 4 outputs are concatenated back to 5120, and a linear map brings them to the latent width $h_G = 4096$.
5. In the decoder, a linear map turns each latent output (4096) into 5120 again, read as 4 key/value vectors of 1280 that byte queries attend to.

The **local decoder** reverses the roles: byte states (starting from the encoder's final byte states) are the queries, and the latent Transformer's patch outputs are the keys and values. Cross-attention comes before each decoder layer, and the last layer feeds a 256-way softmax. For the 8B model the paper lists: encoder 1 layer at width 1280 (20M parameters), latent 32 layers at width 4096 (6.4B), decoder 6 layers at width 1280 (120M).

**Which patch may a byte look at?** Not its own. The predictions for the bytes of patch $j$ cross-attend only to the latent output $o_{j-1}$, which the latent Transformer computed from patches $0$ to $j-1$. If they could see $o_j$, the latent output for the patch pooled from those very bytes, the model would read its own targets. This is the next-step shift you know from the GPT, one level up: a GPT predicts token $t+1$ from position $t$, and BLT predicts patch $j$ from the latent step for patch $j-1$. For the first patch there is no earlier output, so the released code makes the first patch exactly one byte long (in practice the start-of-text byte), and the decoder's patch ids are the patch lengths shifted by one patch.

blocks.title: Decoder mask: which latent output each byte prediction may use

scenes.caption: Rows are the 11 byte predictions for the cat sat; columns are latent outputs. Patch 0 is the single start byte. A 1 means that prediction may attend to that output: each row sees exactly one, the output of the patch before the byte being predicted.

Predicting t, h, e and the space of the_ uses o0, computed from the start byte alone. The local decoder supplies the within-patch context (t before h, and so on) through its own causal self-attention.
Predicting c, a, t, space uses o1, the latent output for the_. The column o2 is pooled from cat_ itself, so allowing it here would leak the targets.
o3, the output for sat, is used by none of these rows: it is the latent model's prediction for whatever patch comes after the text. In training it serves the next patch's bytes.

blocks.md: With hash n-gram embeddings, a 1-layer encoder was enough: in the 1B ablation, 1 encoder plus 9 decoder layers reached 0.822 bits per byte versus 0.844 for 5 plus 5. Spend local layers on the decoder, which must produce every byte.

Encoder: bytes plus hashed n-grams, pooled into patch vectors by masked cross-attention. Latent Transformer: the expensive part, once per patch. Decoder: bytes query the output of the patch before theirs to predict the next byte.

blocks.question: The n-gram 'cat' and some unrelated 3-gram hash to the same slot of $E_3^{hash}$. What happens?
options: Training fails with a key error
They share one embedding vector; the byte embedding and other n-gram sizes still distinguish them
The model falls back to a BPE tokenizer for that word
BLT rehashes until the slot is free
blocks.explain: Hash embeddings accept collisions: both n-grams add the same learned vector. Each position also gets its own byte embedding and five other n-gram lookups, and later layers see the context, so collisions only cost a little. Bigger tables reduce them.

blocks.question: Which part of BLT should get most of the parameters, and why?
options: The latent Transformer, because it runs once per patch, so its cost per byte is divided by the patch size
The local encoder, because it sees every byte
The local decoder, because it has the softmax
The entropy model, because it decides compute
blocks.explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Parameters in the latent model are amortized over P bytes; parameters in local models are paid on every byte. That is why the 8B model has 6.4B latent and only 140M local parameters.

blocks.question: A reimplementation lets each byte of patch $j$ cross-attend to $o_j$ instead of $o_{j-1}$. Training loss drops far below the paper's numbers. What happened?
options: The hash n-gram tables became more effective
The latent output $o_j$ was pooled from the very bytes being predicted, so the targets leaked into the inputs
Cross-attention was cheaper, so the model trained longer
Max-pooling lost information about the patch, which helped regularize
blocks.explain: $o_j$ is computed from patch $j$'s pooled bytes, so a prediction that sees it is reading the answer. The fix is the one-patch shift: bytes of patch $j$ use $o_{j-1}$, as a GPT uses position $t$ to predict token $t+1$.

lessons.title: Generating with patches: the BLT decoding loop and its real cost

blocks.md: Training sees whole sequences at once; generation does not. Take the prompt start byte and let the model write `the cat sat`. A BPE model such as GPT-2's tokenizer splits this into 3 tokens (`the`, ` cat`, ` sat`), so it runs its full network 3 times. BLT must emit 11 bytes, one at a time, and before each byte it has to decide whether that byte starts a new patch. This lesson walks through that loop with the threshold 1.2 patches from lesson 4: the_, cat_, sat.

For every byte, BLT does the following:

1. The **entropy model** reads the byte just produced and computes $H$ for the next byte. It must run online, one step per byte, with its own cache over its 512-byte sliding window.
2. The **local encoder** turns the byte just produced into a byte state (1 layer, with hash n-gram lookups).
3. If $H$ is above the threshold, the next byte starts a patch, so the current patch is finished: the encoder pools it, and the **latent Transformer** runs one step on that patch, extending its cache by one position.
4. The **local decoder** runs one step and predicts the next byte, cross-attending to the newest latent output, which by lesson 5's shift is the output of the patch before the one this byte belongs to.

blocks.title: Which networks run while BLT writes the cat sat

scenes.caption: Byte 0: the start byte is its own first patch, so the latent model runs once on it, and the decoder predicts t. Every byte slot shows entropy and encoder first, an optional latent step, then the decoder.
Bytes 1 to 3 (h, e, space): their entropies are low, so no patch closes. Only the three small networks run; the decoder keeps attending to the start byte's latent output.
Byte 4: the entropy for c is 2.01, so the_ closes. The encoder pools it, the latent model takes its second step, and c, a, t, space are predicted from that output.

Byte 8: s (entropy 1.54) closes cat_, giving the third latent step. 11 bytes cost 3 latent steps but 11 steps each of entropy, encoder and decoder. Simplified: block widths show order, not measured time.
The BPE model for comparison: 3 steps of its full network, one per token (GPT-2's split: the, _cat, _sat), drawn over the bytes each token covers.

blocks.md: Count the work per byte with lesson 1's $2m$ FLOPs per parameter per position, for the 8B configuration at 4.4 bytes per patch. Latent: $2 \times 6.4 / 4.4 = 2.91$ GFLOPs per byte. Local encoder and decoder: $2 \times 0.14 = 0.28$. So BLT costs 3.19 GFLOPs per byte, against 2.91 for a BPE model whose 6.4B network runs once per 4.4-byte token. The entropy model adds $2 \times 0.1 = 0.2$ more, 3.39 in total; the paper's FLOP formula (its equations 13 to 17) counts the encoder, latent, decoder and cross-attention, not the entropy model.

blocks.prompt: BLT and the BPE model need similar FLOPs for the cat sat. Count sequential layer steps instead, MegaByte's model of generation latency, where every layer evaluation costs the same because one position does not fill a GPU. Which needs more, and by how much?
blocks.reveal: BPE: 3 tokens x 32 layers = 96 sequential layer steps. BLT: the latent model also takes 3 steps x 32 = 96, but every one of the 11 bytes also needs the encoder (1 layer) and decoder (6 layers): 96 + 11 x 7 = 173. The entropy model's 14 layers must finish before the decoder knows whether a latent step comes first, adding 11 x 14 = 154, for 327 in all: about 3.4 times the BPE count. FLOP parity says nothing about this serial chain.

blocks.title: Writing the cat sat: compute versus serial steps (8B configs)

scenes.caption: Forward GFLOPs per byte, simplified $2m$ model at 4.4 bytes per token or patch. BLT's local models and entropy model add 10% and then another 7% of the BPE figure.
Sequential layer steps for the 11 bytes (96, 96, 173, 327). The small networks are cheap in FLOPs but run on every byte, one after another, so they dominate the step count.

blocks.md: Several networks now keep caches. The latent Transformer caches keys and values per patch, the decoder per byte, the encoder over its local window, and the entropy model over its 512-byte window. The released reference generator does none of this: `generate_nocache` in `generate_blt.py` re-runs the patcher and the whole model on the full prefix for every new byte, which is simple and correct but far slower than a cached loop.

Batching gets harder too. Serving systems batch many sequences so each step does more work per weight read. In a batch of BLT sequences, patches end at different bytes, so at any byte step only some sequences need a latent step. You either run the latent model on that subset (a smaller, less efficient batch) or make the others wait. MegaByte's fixed $P$ avoids this: every sequence reaches a patch boundary at the same step. MegaByte reports generating 8192 bytes 40% faster than a 350M Transformer with a 1.3B global plus 218M local model trained at equal compute, because most parameters run once per 8 bytes.

The BLT paper is explicit: its FLOP matching is theoretical, and its implementation may not yet match tokenizer-based models in wall-clock time. Equal FLOPs per byte is a claim about arithmetic, not about latency at batch size 1.

A different way to cut sequential byte steps comes from a model that does not patch at all. **MambaByte** (Wang et al., 2024) keeps every byte but uses a Mamba state-space model, whose memory is a fixed-size state rather than a growing attention cache (the keys and values a Transformer keeps for every past position). A state-space model reads a sequence like a recurrent network: at each step it updates a fixed-size state from the previous state and the new input. Mamba (Gu and Dao, 2023) makes that update depend on the input. To speed up generation it drafts with a subword model and verifies with the byte model, a form of speculative decoding: the cheap model proposes several steps ahead, the byte model checks the whole draft in one pass and keeps only what it accepts, reporting a 2.6x speedup over plain MambaByte decoding.

blocks.title: MambaByte speculative decoding: subword draft, byte verify

scenes.caption: The small subword model drafts m subwords autoregressively, recording its hidden states. Drafting in subwords takes far fewer steps than bytes.
The byte model checks all drafted bytes in one parallel scan and finds the bifurcation byte c: the furthest position whose bytes are all in its top-beta candidates.
Verified whole subwords are kept. Bytes after c are dropped, and the byte model generates the corrected subword itself, byte by byte, until a boundary byte such as a space.

add.label: corrected bytes up to a space

scenes.caption: Both models keep their states for the next round: MambaByte's final state and the subword model's state at the bifurcation. The paper reports 2.6x faster decoding than plain MambaByte.

blocks.md: In BLT generation the latent model runs only when a patch closes, but the entropy model, encoder and decoder run on every byte in sequence. Fewer FLOPs per byte and lower latency are different goals; fixed patches, caches and speculative drafting are the levers for the second.

blocks.question: BLT has just emitted the space after cat. The entropy model computes $H = 1.54$ for the next byte, above the threshold 1.2. What runs before the next byte is predicted?
options: Only the local decoder, as for every byte
The encoder pools cat_ into a patch vector, the latent Transformer runs one step on it, then the decoder predicts the next byte using that output
The latent Transformer re-runs on all previous patches
The entropy model is retrained on the new patch
blocks.explain: A high entropy means the next byte starts a new patch, so cat_ is complete. Its pooled vector goes through one cached latent step, and the new output is exactly what the next patch's bytes may attend to under the one-patch shift.

blocks.question: A team serves BLT at batch size 1 and finds it slower per byte than a BPE model with the same latent size, although the FLOPs per byte are within 20%. What best explains this?
options: The 256-way softmax is slower than a 128K-way softmax
Hash n-gram lookups dominate inference
At batch 1 latency follows the number of sequential steps, and the entropy model, encoder and decoder add several layer steps on every byte
The latent model has more layers than the BPE model
blocks.explain: With one sequence, each layer evaluation is a serial step that barely uses the hardware, so the count of sequential steps sets latency. BLT adds 21 small layer steps per byte for the cat sat example (14 entropy, 1 encoder, 6 decoder), on top of the same latent steps.

lessons.title: Results, tradeoffs and where byte models fit

blocks.md: Byte and token models cannot be compared by perplexity, since perplexity is per token. Perplexity is $e$ raised to the average loss per token, so it depends on how much text a token covers: a model with longer tokens makes fewer, harder predictions. BLT therefore reports **bits per byte**, the tokenizer-independent score you computed in lesson 3 for three small models (the formula is repeated below). Dividing by $\ln 2$ works because $\log_2 p = \ln p / \ln 2$. The paper compares models at equal training FLOPs.

Lesson 3's lab shows why the conversion matters. Its BPE model averaged 3.70 nats per token over about 2.97 bytes per token of validation text: $3.70 / (\ln 2 \times 2.97) = 1.80$ bits per byte. Its byte GPT averaged only 1.797 nats per position, which is $1.797 / \ln 2 = 2.59$ bits per byte. The model with the smaller per-position loss is the worse one.

**Compute-optimal** means each model size gets the amount of training data that scaling-law studies of BPE models predict gives the lowest loss for that compute budget. In compute-optimal runs from 1B to 8B parameters on the Llama 2 data, the authors report that entropy-patched BLT matches or beats BPE models trained with the Llama 3 tokenizer. Models with average patches of 6 and 8 bytes land between Llama 2 and Llama 3 tokenizer models while running the big model far less often. The patch-8 model started noticeably worse at 1B but ended better than the Llama 2 tokenizer baseline at 7B.

The next figure averages 7 standard benchmarks: ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge (the AI2 Reasoning Challenge, grade-school science multiple choice), HellaSwag (pick the most plausible ending for a description of an everyday scene), PIQA (Physical Interaction Question Answering, physical common sense), MMLU, and two coding tests, MBPP (Mostly Basic Python Problems) and HumanEval, where generated Python functions must pass unit tests. BLT-1T is the paper's training set of 1 trillion tokens from public sources.

blocks.title: 8B models at equal training FLOPs (BLT-1T data)

scenes.caption: Average over 7 tasks (ARC-E, ARC-C, HellaSwag, PIQA, MMLU, MBPP, HumanEval). Entropy-patched BLT scores 61.1 versus 60.0 for the BPE model.
Bytes per patch (or per token) on the training mix. Space patching averages 6.1 bytes, so it uses fewer global steps, and pays about 2 points of average score.

blocks.md: The more interesting result is at **fixed inference cost**. For a token model, the inference budget fixes the model size. For BLT, a longer patch frees compute to grow the latent model. Starting from Llama 2 tokenizer models of 470M and 3.6B, the authors built inference-FLOP-matched models: entropy patch size 6 allows a 1.2x to 1.3x larger model, and patch size 8 a 1.6x to 1.7x larger one.

blocks.title: Model size at equal inference FLOPs per byte

scenes.caption: Smaller budget class: 470M, 450M, 610M and 760M non-embedding parameters all cost the same per byte at inference.
Larger class: 3.6B, 3.9B, 5.2B, 6.6B (shown in millions). BPE models win at small training budgets, then BLT overtakes them; the crossover was at about 2.5x to 3x the compute-optimal data.

blocks.md: Reading bytes also changes what the model knows. On noised HellaSwag (random case, dropped or repeated characters, all caps, spaced-out letters) BLT averaged 64.3 versus 56.9 for the BPE model trained on the same 1T tokens. On CUTE, a benchmark of spelling and character manipulation, BLT scored 54.1 versus 27.5, including 99.9 on spelling. It also beat the BPE model on low-resource translation (FLORES-101) by 2 BLEU into English. FLORES-101 is a test set of the same sentences translated into 101 languages; low-resource languages are those with little training text. BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) scores a translation from 0 to 100 by how many of its word n-grams also appear in a reference translation.

blocks.title: Robustness and character-level skill (8B models)

scenes.caption: Clean HellaSwag: 79.1, 80.7 and 80.6. On clean text BLT matches the BPE models.
Noised HellaSwag average: 56.9, 64.3, 64.3. Noise hurts everyone, but BLT trained on 1T tokens matches Llama 3.1 trained on far more data.
CUTE (character manipulation): 27.5, 20.0, 54.1. More data did not help Llama 3.1 here; seeing the bytes did.

blocks.md: Limitations the authors list: their FLOP matching is theoretical and the implementation may not yet match token models in wall-clock time; the entropy model is trained separately rather than end to end; and they borrowed BPE scaling-law data ratios that may not be optimal for BLT. BPE still won word deletion and word insertion on CUTE.

You do not have to train from scratch. BLT can be initialized from a token model: the authors copied Llama 3.1's non-embedding weights into the latent Transformer and trained it at one tenth the learning rate of the local models. At the same training FLOPs this raised MMLU from 25.2 (BLT from scratch) to 63.7, against 66.3 for the original Llama 3.1.

Byte models trade a tokenizer for an extra design choice: how to group bytes. With learned, entropy-based patches, BLT matched BPE models at 8B for equal training FLOPs, improved robustness and spelling, and turned patch size into a knob that trades steps for model size.

blocks.question: You serve a model under a fixed inference FLOP budget per byte. Why can BLT use a bigger model than a BPE model in the same budget?
options: Byte embeddings are smaller than token embeddings
The entropy model replaces some latent layers
Bigger average patches mean fewer latent steps per byte, so each step can afford more parameters
BLT skips the softmax at inference
blocks.explain: Cost per byte is about 2(m_g/P + m_l). Raising P from about 3.7 (Llama 2 tokens) to 8 lowers the m_g/P term, so m_g can grow while cost per byte stays fixed: 760M versus 470M in the paper's small class. BPE can only lengthen tokens by growing the vocabulary.

blocks.question: A product mainly processes noisy user text (typos, odd casing) in many languages, and needs character-level edits. Which statement best matches the evidence in this course?
options: A BPE model with more training data will close the gap on character tasks
Byte-level models with patching are a strong fit; they were more robust to noise and far better at character manipulation
Byte models only help for English
Byte models are always faster at inference than BPE models
blocks.explain: BLT beat a same-data BPE model by 7.4 points on noised HellaSwag and by 26.6 on CUTE, while Llama 3.1, trained on far more data, scored lower on CUTE. Speed depends on patch size and implementation; the authors note wall-clock parity is not yet shown.

lessons.title: Learning where to cut: from character models to H-Net

blocks.md: In BLT, a frozen 100M-parameter byte model decides every patch boundary, and the big model must live with those cuts. If `on_the_` would be better as two patches for the latent Transformer, no gradient can tell the entropy model so. BLT's authors list this as a limitation. This lesson places BLT in the longer line of models that shorten character or byte sequences, and then studies H-Net (Hwang et al., 2025), which learns its boundaries together with the rest of the network.

**CANINE** (Clark et al., 2021) is an encoder like BERT that reads Unicode code points instead of word pieces. It embeds each code point with 8 hash functions, each looking up its own table of 16k buckets, and concatenates the 8 pieces of 96 dimensions into one 768-wide vector, an ancestor of BLT's hash n-gram tables. One layer of *local* attention (each character attends only within its 128-character block) mixes neighbours, then a **strided convolution** (a learned filter applied to a window of 4 characters, moved 4 positions at a time) shortens the sequence 4 times before the deep Transformer stack. The cut is fixed: every 4 characters, whatever they are. On TyDi QA, a multilingual question-answering benchmark, its best variant beat a comparable multilingual BERT by 5.7 F1 (a 0 to 100 score of answer overlap) with fewer parameters.

**Charformer** (Tay et al., 2021) makes the cut soft. Its GBST module (gradient-based subword tokenization) pools candidate blocks of 1 to 4 bytes at every position, scores each block size with a small learned layer, and takes a softmax over the sizes, so each position becomes a weighted mix of its candidate blocks. A fixed mean-pool then shortens the sequence by a set rate. The choice of block is learned by gradient descent, but the final downsampling rate is fixed.

**Hourglass** (Nawrot et al., 2021) is a decoder that shortens, processes and upsamples: a few full-length layers, then pooling by a factor $k$, many shortened layers, then upsampling back. To stay causal it shifts the sequence right by $k-1$ before shortening, the same problem MegaByte solves with its padding patch. **Dynamic token pooling** (Nawrot et al., 2022) replaces the fixed $k$ with a boundary predictor, a small network giving each position a probability of ending a segment, trained jointly with the language model through a Gumbel-sigmoid relaxation (a differentiable stand-in for a coin flip), or supervised by a Unigram tokenizer, by spikes in conditional entropy, or by whitespace.

**MrT5** (Kallini et al., 2024) shortens ByT5's encoder from inside. After a fixed early encoder layer, a **delete gate** (one linear layer and a scaled sigmoid, about $2d$ extra parameters) gives every byte a score between 0 and $-30$. During training the score is added to the attention logits, softly masking bytes; at inference, bytes below $-15$ are removed. A tunable regularizer sets how much is deleted. It reports sequences up to 75% shorter with accuracy comparable to ByT5.

blocks.title: Who decides where a byte sequence is cut

scenes.caption: Fixed rates cut every k units regardless of content: cheap and simple to batch, but a word lands differently each time.
Hand-written rules cut at spaces (SpaceByte) or at words and groups of words (AU-Net, covered at the end of this lesson). They match English well and struggle with scripts without spaces.
BLT uses a separately trained model's uncertainty. Boundaries adapt to content, but the main model's loss cannot change them.

Learned designs let the language-model loss shape the cuts: soft block mixtures, a boundary predictor, and H-Net's similarity router, which this lesson builds next. (MrT5's delete gate also learns, but removes bytes rather than cutting.)

blocks.md: **H-Net** has the shape of a U-Net, the image architecture that narrows and then widens again. Bytes go through an **encoder** (a few Mamba or Transformer layers at byte level), a **chunking layer** picks which positions to keep, a large **main network** runs on the kept positions, a **dechunking layer** expands back to every byte, and a **decoder** predicts the next byte. The main network can itself be an H-Net, giving 2 stages of chunking (for example bytes, then word-like chunks, then larger units). The new part is the router that decides what to keep.

blocks.tex: q_t = W_q \hat{x}_t,\quad k_t = W_k \hat{x}_t,\quad p_t = \tfrac{1}{2}\Big(1 - \frac{q_t^\top k_{t-1}}{\lVert q_t\rVert\,\lVert k_{t-1}\rVert}\Big),\quad b_t = \mathbb{1}\{p_t \ge 0.5\}
blocks.caption: Routing module. x-hat_t is the encoder output at byte t; p_1 = 1 so the sequence starts with a boundary. b_t = 1 keeps byte t as the start of a new chunk.

blocks.md: In words: project the current byte's state to a query and the previous byte's state to a key, and measure their **cosine similarity**, the dot product of the two vectors divided by their lengths, from $-1$ (opposite) to $1$ (same direction). Similar neighbours (cosine near 1) give $p_t$ near 0: same chunk. A sharp change in context (cosine below 0) gives $p_t$ above 0.5: start a new chunk. The kept positions are simply selected, no pooling, and $p_t$ uses only bytes up to $t$, so the router is causal.

blocks.title: Routing 6 bytes: cosine to boundary

scenes.caption: Assumed cosine similarities between each byte's query and the previous byte's key (illustrative values, not from a trained model). The first byte has no predecessor.
p_t = (1 - cos) / 2. Inside cat the states are similar, so p is 0.20 and 0.15. Moving from the space to o flips direction (cos -0.5), so p = 0.75.
b_t = 1 where p is at least 0.5: c (always) and o. Two chunks, cat_ and on, so the main network runs on 2 of 6 positions.
Confidence c_t is p_t at a boundary and 1 - p_t elsewhere. The space, at p = 0.45, is the least confident decision: 0.55. The smoothing step and the gradient both act most where confidence is low.

blocks.md: A hard choice $b_t$ has no gradient, so H-Net adds three pieces. The **smoothing module** blends each chunk's main-network output with the previous one using an exponential moving average weighted by $P_t$, the boundary probability of the kept position, so a doubtful boundary (P near 0.5) mixes in earlier context while a confident one (P near 1) passes through. The **upsampler** repeats each chunk's vector for every byte until the next boundary and multiplies it by the confidence $c_t$, rounded to 1 in the forward pass by a **straight-through estimator** (it acts as 1 going forward but passes gradients as if it were $c_t$). A residual from the encoder gives each byte its own detail back.

blocks.caption: Left: smoothing over chunks. Right: ratio loss, with F = fraction of positions kept (sum of b_t / L), G = mean p_t, N = target bytes per chunk. Added to the language-model loss with weight 0.03.

blocks.md:
The third piece is the **ratio loss**, which plays the role of BLT's threshold calibration, inside training. $F$ counts the kept positions and has no gradient; $G$, the mean boundary probability, does. In the example, $F = 2/6 = 0.333$ and $G = 2.8/6 = 0.467$. Its slope with respect to $G$ is $\frac{N}{N-1}\big((N-1)F - (1-F)\big)$, so the sign depends only on whether $F$ is above or below $1/N$:

- Target $N = 3$: $F = 1/3$ exactly, the slope is 0 and the loss is 1.0, its value at the target.
- Target $N = 4$: $F > 1/4$, slope $+0.44$ (loss 1.096): gradient descent lowers the $p_t$, removing boundaries.
- Target $N = 2$: $F < 1/2$, slope $-0.67$ (loss 1.022): gradient descent raises the $p_t$.

blocks.prompt: With target N = 2, the ratio loss pushes every boundary probability up. Which of the four non-boundary bytes a, t, _, n will cross 0.5 and become a chunk start first?
blocks.reveal: The space, whose p is already 0.45; a needs to rise from 0.20, t from 0.15 and n from 0.25. Then the chunks would be cat, _ and on. In a real run the language-model loss pushes back as well: the ratio loss only sets how many chunks, and the prediction loss decides which positions are worth a main-network step.

blocks.md: Compare BLT. BLT's boundaries come from a separate model trained only to predict bytes, and the patch size is set by a threshold calibrated once the entropy model is trained and fixed while BLT trains; H-Net's come from a router trained by the final loss, with the average size steered by $N$ during training. BLT pools a patch with cross-attention; H-Net keeps one encoder state per chunk and relies on the residual and decoder for the rest. When a chunk's vector is selected at its first byte, its main-network output is used for the bytes inside that chunk, causal by construction.

**AU-Net** (Videau et al., 2025), also from Meta, keeps the U-shape but does not learn the cuts: a regular expression pools at word boundaries in stage 2, every 2 words in stage 3 and every 4 words in stage 4, so deeper stages predict further ahead. Its authors note the rule must be stable when bytes are appended on the right (the incremental property of lesson 4), that it suits Latin scripts, and that it lags BPE on Chinese MMLU.

What each paper claims at matched compute, in its own setup (not directly comparable): BLT matches BPE models with the Llama 3 tokenizer up to 8B at equal training FLOPs. H-Net reports a 1-stage byte model beating a BPE Transformer when compute and data are matched, and a 2-stage model matching a BPE Transformer twice its size. AU-Net reports shallow hierarchies on par with strong BPE baselines. Scales, data and baselines differ.

The design space for byte models is who decides the cut: a fixed rate, a hand-written rule, a separate model (BLT), or the model's own loss (H-Net's cosine router plus a ratio loss). Learned cuts remove BLT's separately trained entropy model, at the cost of new machinery to make a discrete choice trainable.

blocks.question: During H-Net training with target N = 4, a batch keeps 40% of positions as chunk starts. What does the ratio loss do?
options: Pushes boundary probabilities down, since F = 0.4 is above 1/N = 0.25
Nothing, because F has no gradient
Pushes boundary probabilities up, to reach 4 chunks per byte
Raises the cosine threshold from 0.5 to 0.6
blocks.explain: The slope with respect to G is N/(N-1) x ((N-1)F - (1-F)) = 4/3 x (1.2 - 0.6) = 0.8, positive, so descent lowers G and fewer positions reach 0.5. F has no gradient itself, but it sets the sign; the threshold 0.5 never changes.

blocks.question: Which of these lets the language-model loss itself change where a byte sequence is cut?
options: CANINE's stride-4 convolution
BLT's entropy patching
H-Net's routing module
AU-Net's regular-expression splits
blocks.explain: H-Net's router is trained end to end through the smoothing module, the straight-through confidence and the ratio loss. CANINE's rate is fixed, AU-Net's split is a rule, and BLT's entropy model is trained separately and frozen.
